overview: This map record combines a troubled era rather than one state lasting from 1914 to 1938. The independent Armenian Republic existed from 1918 to 1920, followed by Soviet rule. The imported “Sasanian E” alias is wrong. Its 1930 outline lies far west across much of present-day eastern Turkey; it must not be read as Soviet Armenia’s border or proof that a proposed postwar Armenian frontier became reality.

periods.title: Imperial borderlands at war
periods.summary: Armenian communities lived on both sides of the Ottoman-Russian conflict. War and genocide uprooted families.

periods.title: The First Republic
periods.summary: An independent republic developed institutions while facing war and disputed boundaries.

periods.title: Early Soviet Armenia
periods.summary: Soviet rule followed in late 1920. Armenia entered the Transcaucasian federation in 1922 and became a separate Soviet union republic in 1936.

items.text: In 1914, Armenian society was divided across imperial borders. Russian forces and Ottoman forces fought through the Caucasus and eastern Anatolia. The modern country and the Ottoman Armenian communities affected by that war were connected, but they were not identical territories or populations.

The Armenian genocide destroyed Ottoman Armenian communities in 1915 and 1916 through mass killing, deportation and deliberately lethal conditions. Survivors and refugees carried memories, skills and family ties into new places. Their later lives belong to this history alongside the violence inflicted on them.

The First Republic’s 1919 election sent three women to an eighty-member parliament. Katarine Zalyan-Manukyan, Perchuhi Partizpanyan-Barseghyan and Varvara Sahakyan participated in a new public institution during an emergency. Voting rights and elected office opened possibilities beyond traditional household responsibilities.

Katarine Zalyan-Manukyan worked on the Medical-Sanitary Commission, including refugees’ needs. Varvara Sahakyan also worked with people left homeless by the genocide. Medicine, shelter and family survival were immediate political tasks, not subjects that could wait until borders and governments settled down.

sections.title: A university and an Armenian sentence

items.text: A law of 16 May 1919 established the university. Because Yerevan lacked a suitable building, the opening took place at Alexandropol’s trade school on 31 January 1920. A national university began by borrowing space: an ambitious idea did not arrive with a ready-made campus.

For the opening, a one-day newspaper presented professors’ speeches and the first semester’s timetable. Its sales supported a fund for students with little money. Publishing, public celebration and practical help for students were brought together in the same small object.

Written Armenian: Գիտութիւնն ոյժ է ,  Gitutʿiwnn oyž ē, “Science is power.” This is the university museum’s transcription of the motto in the newspaper issued on 31 January 1920. Its historical spelling is preserved; the museum’s English account supplies the translation.

Teaching required books as well as buildings. The university’s history records professors translating textbooks in 1922. Students attended laboratory work and seminars alongside lectures, making scientific education a matter of things to handle and test as well as words to hear.

Laboratories obtained microscopes and other costly equipment from abroad. In 1926, physiologist Leon Orbeli helped purchase laboratory equipment. Scientific work depended on these networks of people and instruments; declaring a faculty was only the start of making it function.

At Alexandropol’s relief orphanages, schooling and vocational training shared the day with organized play. An archive photograph shows girls doing gymnastics in the yard around 1920. These institutions served children affected by catastrophe; their routines were not a description of every Armenian childhood.

The orphanage gardens supplied practical lessons, but children also filled them with little mud houses and play spaces. Archived photographs show children building and inspecting these miniature structures. A gardening lesson could apparently acquire its own tiny neighborhood.

Food relief could begin far away in a grocery shop. In 1921, American shopkeepers displayed flour barrels and collected contributions for Near East Relief. Alexandropol’s orphanages used flour in large quantities for bread, although the surviving account does not identify the exact bread recipe.

sections.title: Remaking a city and remembering its costs

items.text: Alexander Tamanyan’s 1924 plan imagined Yerevan for about 150,000 residents. Broad streets and open squares reorganized the capital. The plan shows how a government could try to shape daily movement, public gatherings and future growth through the layout of a city.

During the 1930s, Yerevan gained electricity, sewers, running water and paved streets. These works changed practical city life, from lighting to moving water and waste. The evidence describes urban infrastructure, not a promise that every home immediately had its own bathroom.

Modernization also removed older places. Yerevan’s ruined fortress, the old ruler’s palace and open bazaar were cleared away during rebuilding. A new capital gained facilities while losing parts of its earlier streetscape; progress and preservation did not always travel together.

Educational growth existed alongside Stalinist repression. University rector Kamsar Arakelyan was arrested on 8 January 1938, later imprisoned and exiled. He was cleared in 1955 when the case was found to lack a crime. Political terror could overturn a scholarly career and a family’s life.

ending.text: The independent republic ended in 1920 amid Turkish attacks and the Soviet takeover. Armenian institutions continued in a different political system. The map’s 1938 cutoff ends this imported interval, not Soviet Armenia or Armenian society; Soviet rule lasted until 1991.
